article.articleHeadline: WHO official: Africa's Ebola outbreak may be far larger than official figures.
article.articleSummary:
- On July 10, 2026, WHO Emergency Programme head Chikwe Ihekweazu warned that Africa’s Bundibugyo ebolavirus outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo may be far larger than official tallies, with many infections undetected. In some areas of the DRC, roughly four of every five new Ebola cases have no known link to existing patients, and the outbreak’s true size could be two to four times higher than reported. About 90% of confirmed Ebola cases remain in Ituri Province, though transmission has spread to neighboring provinces. The outbreak is caused by Bundibugyo ebolavirus, for which there is currently no vaccine or specific therapeutic option. The statement highlights under-detection and continued spread despite containment efforts.
- Bundibugyo-strain Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) continues in Ituri Province, with Bunia as epicenter. Since May 15, 1,561 cases have been confirmed and 506 deaths reported, over 500 fatalities overall. Frontline workers—epidemiological surveillance, safety and security, community outreach, and burial teams—have begun striking over unpaid wages and bonuses, while Bunia airport closure hampers response. Ebola cases have reached the rebel-held zone, including a single infection in Goma, raising concern about spread to M23-controlled areas such as Goma and Bukavu. WHO and the DRC have launched a clinical trial in affected regions to test MBP134 monoclonal antibodies, remdesivir, or a combination; enrollment has begun, with meaningful results potentially taking several months 
- A U.S. citizen working for a humanitarian organization in Democratic Republic of the Congo has tested positive for Bundibugyo virus, a form of Ebola, CDC said. The patient’s name was not released, and this marks the second American known to have contracted Ebola in current outbreak. First case, Dr. Peter Stafford, was evacuated to Germany in May and has since recovered. Congo outbreak—declared May 15 and described as Africa’s fastest-growing Ebola outbreak—reports 1,830 confirmed cases and 648 deaths, with cases in Uganda. Bundibugyo virus has no approved vaccine or treatment. CDC is coordinating with the employer, U.S. agencies, Congolese public health authorities, and local partners to limit spread via contact tracing and risk assessments for high-risk exposures. - Bundibugyo Ebola virus infection detected in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) involving an American humanitarian worker. The patient, affiliated with a local relief organization operating in the DRC, tested positive for Bundibugyo Ebola virus. CDC confirmed the case on Friday and said it is coordinating with the worker’s organization, other U.S. federal agencies, and Congolese partners to prevent further spread, including tracing high-risk close contacts. The U.S. State Department acknowledged the case on Saturday and is providing assistance to the affected American citizen, while privacy protections limit details on the patient’s condition and treatment. The response emphasizes containment, surveillance, and protection of workers in the region amid Ebola activity in the DRC.
- Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, dominated by Ituri Province, with 1,792 confirmed cases and 625 deaths reported as of 12 July 2026; about 90% of cases are in Ituri, with spread to North Kivu, South Kivu and Tshopo. WHO notes that roughly 80% of new infections cannot be linked to known cases, indicating extensive community transmission. Bunia shows consistently high test positivity, signifying ongoing transmission despite progress in other areas. The figures align with an earlier report citing 1,759 confirmed cases and 600 deaths. This laboratory-confirmed outbreak emphasizes Ebola infection, with no specific infection source detailed beyond unlinked cases and no exported/imported case information provided.

Laboratory typing on 38 samples found 26 positives: 11 Dengue virus serotype 1 (D1) and 15 serotype 2 (D2). Kim Long Ward accounted for the most cases (53, 37% of Hue’s total). The rise is linked to high vector indices, many outdoor water containers, ongoing urbanization, tourism, and festivals, with uneven community participation in control measures. The Đắk Lắk CDC notes intensified collaboration with local health services to curb transmission during the rainy-season peak, prioritizing vector control, sanitation, and public awareness. article.articleHeadline: Letters to the Editor: Ebola Without Borders | El Diario Vasco
article.articleSummary: Letter to the Editor: Ebola Without Borders highlights the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, urging reflection that behind every figure lies a life lost and a family shattered. In a globalized world with thousands crossing borders daily, the piece warns that a severe epidemic cannot be confined to a single region, and no continent is fully protected from viral spread. The author, Ander Murillo of Ordizia, argues that Europe should move beyond observation. It calls for reinforced epidemiological surveillance, strengthened sanitary controls, increased international cooperation, and intensified support to affected countries to contain a highly dangerous disease. The letter stresses that viruses travel with people, and that robust, collaborative public health responses are essential to prevent cross-border transmission of Ebola.

Authorities plan to intensify prevention and control, including launching the second phase of the epizootic vaccination campaign and maintaining national animal vaccination programs to protect remaining livestock, limit human transmission, and safeguard rural livelihoods. Rabies is a viral infection typically transmitted to humans via dog bites or saliva from infected animals and is almost always fatal once symptoms appear. The article calls for heightened awareness, animal vaccination, and prompt care for exposed people to prevent further spread in Sankuru.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola in Bunia: Strengthening Movement Controls in Light of the Risk of Importation - ACP
article.articleSummary: Ebola virus disease risk prompts strengthened community movement controls in Muzi-Pela, Bunia, Ituri Province, northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. Authorities register all arrivals from Ebola-affected Djugu and other zones, with Muzi-Pela housing about 90% of Djugu nationals, including displaced persons. Daily entries from Lopa, Mongbwalu, Nizi and nearby areas are recorded to identify people with suspicious signs and to relay information to response teams. On average, more than 50 new arrivals are registered weekly. Led by 19 avenue chiefs, this surveillance aims to detect potential cases early and interrupt transmission chains as part of the Ebola response. Local market-avenue leadership emphasizes community sensitization on barrier measures and prompt reporting of suspected cases or unusual deaths. The effort, supported by the Judith Suminwa Foundation and the Prime Minister, seeks sustained community collaboration to prevent importation and spread of Ebola in Ituri.

article.articleHeadline: 12 de Octubre tests an oral vaccine against an Ebola variant in mice.
article.articleSummary: Madrid’s 12 de Octubre Public Hospital shows an oral vaccine against Ebola Zaire variant is viable in mice, using virus-like particles with no genetic material to induce immunity. Oral delivery could overcome cold chain and healthcare workforce needs inherent to injectables. In two funded studies (Community of Madrid, European Union, Instituto de Salud Carlos III), vaccinated mice had a 67% survival rate; a single dose generated neutralizing antibodies against the Ebola glycoprotein, with a three-dose regimen providing stronger responses. Vaccinated animals also exhibited slower disease progression, less weight loss, and significantly lower viral loads in blood and organs (spleen, liver, lungs). The approach remains preclinical and not yet for humans, targeting Zaire ebolavirus, while the current central African outbreak is caused by Bundibugyo ebolavirus in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda. As of July 8, DRC reported 1,792 cases and 625 deaths; Uganda 20 cases and 2 deaths, with Ituri most affected.

article.articleSummary: Cholera outbreak in Kabimba, Kalemie Territory, Tanganyika, is now under control as of July 9, 2026. The first case was reported July 4; 16 cases have been recorded, with three patients still under treatment and the others discharged. Investigations tie the outbreak to consumption of untreated water from Lake Tanganyika, Kabimba’s main drinking-water source. Authorities urge enhanced hygiene, water treatment, boiling water when disinfectants aren’t available, and improved sanitation to prevent resurgence. The Red Cross and CONCERN assisted with disinfection of affected homes. article.articleHeadline: Trust Becomes Stronger Than Fear": On the Frontlines of DRC's 17th Ebola Outbreak, Aid Workers Battle a Second Epidemic -- Doubt | Best African News Online
article.articleSummary: DRC's 17th Ebola outbreak hits North Kivu and Ituri as funding cuts hollow the response and a collapsing health system struggles to protect communities. CARE and partners have reached over 210,000 people with prevention messages and deployed 533 trained community health workers across 47 health areas in 14 health zones, but this reach covers only a small fraction of the millions at risk. Frontline responders describe a dual crisis: the virus and a deep erosion of trust, with residents in Mugunga (Goma) and Hero Mandibe (Ituri) reporting suspicion that aid workers are making money again. Women and girls bear the steepest barriers to care, protection from violence, and mental health support. An imported case saw a woman infected arrive in Goma from Ituri, prompting isolation and reinforced Sake entry screenings.

article.articleHeadline: The WHO's Africa Emergency Director, reporting from Congo: "Everything points to this being the worst Ebola outbreak to date."

Bunia serves as the epicenter of the crisis. Belizaire—a Haitian physician educated in Cuba with a PhD in Epidemiology and Public Health from Spain—has led responses to AIDS in Haiti, Ebola in West Africa, yellow fever in Angola, and dengue plus Crimean-Congo fever in Mauritania. She warns that effective outbreak control must blend local customs and beliefs with scientific measures to avoid resistance and distrust. Her larger aim beyond containment is to improve people’s lives after the outbreak, ensuring access to food, water and latrines.

article.articleHeadline: Hantavirus outbreak offers lessons for the next pandemic
article.articleSummary: Andes virus hantavirus outbreak aboard expedition ship MV Hondius (May 2–13, 2026) caused 13 cases and 3 deaths among passengers and crew from 23 countries, with the voyage sailing from the southern tip of South America toward the Canary Islands. Investigators traced the source to a Dutch birdwatcher who contracted the virus on land in Chile and Argentina and infected others aboard before dying. Andes virus is the only hantavirus known to spread between people, via respiratory droplets; most hantaviruses are rodent-borne. The outbreak remained contained, with 16 contacts monitored in Nebraska and some exposed individuals quarantined in the United States, while Canada monitored at home. Public fear outpaced evidence; the response relied on WHO guidance, CDC leadership, and academic collaborators. The episode contrasts with a larger Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (500+ cases, ~100 deaths) and with a 2018–2019 Argentine Andes outbreak (34 cases, 11 deaths) stopped by self-isolation.

article.articleHeadline: Experts warn of the unpredictable burden caused by dengue fever in Dong Nai
article.articleSummary: Dengue fever in Dong Nai, Vietnam, remains a major concern amid the monsoon. By end-June 2026, Dong Nai reported 4,413 dengue cases, down 24.8% year-on-year, yet monthly cases rose to 527 in June, up about 30% from May. The province leads national dengue deaths, accounting for 3 of 7 fatalities since January. Contributing factors include its border proximity to Ho Chi Minh City, dense transport networks, numerous industrial zones and crowded accommodations, plus construction-site pits and standing water that foster Aedes aegypti mosquitoes and virus transmission. Early dengue presents like flu; by days 3–7, defervescence may herald severe complications (shock, hemorrhage, multi-organ failure). Warning signs include lethargy, reduced urination, severe abdominal or hepatic pain, skin rash, and cold extremities. Healthcare burden is high: 10,000+ outpatient visits annually, ~3,000 hospitalizations, ~1,000 severe cases with organ involvement; costs for severe cases can reach 200–750 million VND. An ongoing June 2026 public health talk emphasizes prevention and early treatment.

article.articleHeadline: Health department reports travel-related dengue case in Oahu resident

The most recent case is an Oahu resident who was exposed while traveling in a dengue-endemic region. Hawaii Department of Health teams have been deployed to inspect and implement mosquito-control measures in the area; officials say the risk of local transmission remains low given the circumstances. Dengue virus is transmitted by mosquitoes and is common in tropical and subtropical areas of Central and South America, Asia, the Middle East, Africa, and Pacific and Caribbean islands. Countries with higher-than-usual activity include Samoa, Vietnam, Colombia, Cambodia, Maldives, Mali, New Caledonia, Timor-Leste, Bolivia, and Guyana. Travelers should review travel guidance 4–6 weeks before travel. Symptoms include fever, nausea, vomiting, rash, and body aches. If traveled and symptomatic, contact a healthcare provider or call DOH at (808) 586-4586.

article.articleHeadline: Livestock farming maintains growth amid rising disease pressure.
article.articleSummary: Vietnam's livestock sector maintains growth amid disease pressure in 2026. African swine fever outbreaks reach 697 across 28 provinces, up about 60% year-on-year. Avian influenza outbreaks occur in 15 provinces, rising 3.8-fold. Lumpy skin disease outbreaks and cattle infections decline, though rabies remains in several localities, demanding ongoing surveillance. The pig herd grew about 2.2%, supporting pork output of roughly 2.86 million tonnes in six months, with notable gains in Lam Dong (5.5%), Ho Chi Minh City (4.5%), Dong Nai (4.2%), Phu Tho (3.8%), and Bac Ninh (3.1%). Poultry sectors show robust growth: total fowl stock up 3.1% by end-June; live poultry meat output about 1.3 million tonnes (+5.6%), and eggs ~10.8 billion (+2.6%). To ensure supply, authorities urge vaccination, biosecurity, transport/slaughter/trade monitoring, vaccine stocking, routine disinfection, and strict control of prohibited substances and antibiotics; promote traceability and safe, connected value chains.

article.articleHeadline: Technology to Combat Dengue Arrives in São Carlos and Promises to Reduce Transmission.
article.articleSummary: São Carlos, São Paulo, Brazil launches Wolbachia-based control to reduce transmission of Dengue, Zika, and Chikungunya by Aedes aegypti. The municipal Health Surveillance Department advances preparations after selecting the city in 2025 based on vector infestation. The program releases Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes (Wolbitos) in defined areas; over generations, the bacterium spreads, lowering viral replication in mosquitoes and transmission risk. First releases are planned for September, occurring gradually over about 26 weeks, with monitoring of Wolbachia establishment and epidemiological analyses to assess disease reduction. Community engagement is essential, including education and household surveys before releases. The technology is considered safe and WHO-approved, complementing existing measures like breeding-site elimination and vector control. Outpatient and international precedents report substantial reductions: Niterói (Dengue 89%, Chikungunya 60%, Zika 37%), Campo Grande Dengue 63%; Vietnam 86%, Indonesia 77%, Colombia 97%, Australia 97%.

article.articleHeadline: Testing drugs that could treat dengue
article.articleSummary: Two potential dengue drugs are moving toward trials as the Dengue Alliance (DNDi) with Brazil, India, Malaysia, and Thailand targets antivirals and host-directed therapies to curb severe inflammation. Dengue remains without a direct cure; current care is supportive. The virus stays in the body about 10 days, with fever lasting roughly 4–5 days after onset, making early treatment crucial. Severe disease often results from the inflammatory response, causing plasma leakage and circulatory shock after the virus is cleared. The Alliance plans to test two candidates by 2027. One is a monoclonal antibody developed by Serum Institute of India, to be trialed in India and at alliance sites; Malaysia coordinates trials via the Health Ministry, with Hospital Raja Permaisuri Bainun in Ipoh as a primary site and other clinics. IV administration takes about an hour for dengue patients aged five and up. The aim is to reduce complications, deaths, and downtime.

article.articleSummary: As of 11 July 2026, three howler monkeys were spotted at Desengano State Park in Santa Maria Madalena, interior Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Park ranger Mateus Guinancio observed a family—father, mother, and a dependent infant—and photographed one individual. The sighting is rare and a biodiversity milestone for Rio de Janeiro, as the species has suffered drastic population declines and remains endangered. The howler monkey is listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN. Past drivers of decline include habitat loss and a Yellow Fever outbreak between 2016 and 2018. The apparent resurgence in the wild is attributed to conservation actions and signals the species' recovery. These primates, emblematic of the Atlantic Forest, live in canopy groups and play a crucial ecological role by feeding on leaves, fruits, and flowers, aiding seed dispersal and forest regeneration.

article.articleHeadline: Special Region of Yogyakarta records 25 leprosy cases, learn the symptoms and how to prevent them.
article.articleSummary: Leprosy (Mycobacterium leprae) continues to burden Indonesia, with the Special Region of Yogyakarta (DIY) reporting 25 new cases through the second quarter of 2026. Globally, nearly 200,000 new cases occur each year, and Indonesia remains among the top three countries by case load alongside India and Brazil, accounting for about 71.9% of global cases; Indonesia logged about 15,000 new cases in 2023. In DIY, early symptoms to watch include skin patches that are numb or discolored, thickened peripheral nerves, numbness in hands or feet, muscle weakness, and non-healing wounds. Transmission typically requires close, prolonged contact with untreated patients; casual interactions such as handshakes or sharing utensils are unlikely to spread the disease. MDT provides free treatment for 6–12 months. Stigma remains a barrier; authorities are strengthening active surveillance, early case finding, and public education, including collaboration with Kominfo to improve health literacy.

article.articleHeadline: Device detects avian influenza antibodies in 6 minutes.
article.articleSummary: Brazilian researchers unveiled a microfluidic electronic tongue capable of detecting antibodies against H5N1 avian influenza in about 6 minutes. The device employs a multiplex of sensors and renewable-source proteins, with artificial intelligence interpreting electrical signals to indicate immune response to H5N1. In tests, it demonstrated high detection capability and about 99% accuracy in differentiating H5N1-positive samples from those associated with other common avian diseases, with no false positives reported. The platform, described in the April ACS Applied Nano Materials paper, could be deployed in veterinary clinics, poultry farms, and health-surveillance centers, and may be adaptable to other pathogens, including human health applications. Coordinated by Osvaldo Novais de Oliveira Junior (IFSC-USP), the work involved Embrapa Instrumentação, UF Amazonas, IFSP, and international partners, with FAPESP funding. Early detection is crucial to control outbreaks and limit trade disruptions for poultry producers.

article.articleHeadline: Brazilian research identifies proteins that could broaden the protection provided by malaria vaccines
article.articleSummary: Malaria vaccine research from Federal University of Minas Gerais (CTVacinas), led by Camila Barbosa and Luna de Lacerda, published in Nature, identifies 453 peptides from 166 Plasmodium vivax proteins as novel vaccine candidates. Using immunopeptidomics, the team shows reticulocytes can present parasite antigens via HLA class I, enabling CD8+ T cell responses and challenging long-held assumptions. The targets are primarily internal proteins—ribosomal proteins, histones, and ETRAMPs—that mutate slowly, offering stable vaccine targets. About 71% of these proteins are conserved across Plasmodium species and 75% are expressed in life cycle stages (mosquito, liver, blood, hypnozoites). Validation in P. vivax and P. falciparum patient samples, non-human primates, and mice reveals robust CD8+ T cell responses; two antigens confer protection in animals. Analyses included samples from Brazil, Mali, and the United States, highlighting potential for universal malaria vaccines. Notably, it is the first Nature paper from a study conducted by Brazilian women.

article.articleHeadline: Child bitten by a bat at a Betim daycare.
article.articleSummary: Rabies exposure in Betim, Minas Gerais, Brazil: A 3-year-old child was bitten on the foot by a bat hidden inside a shoe at a daycare in Petrovale, after the animal presumably entered the footwear. The child received rabies post-exposure prophylaxis and was discharged with instructions to complete the vaccine doses in Betim; the incident occurred on Monday, July 6, 2026. A family member killed the bat, which had contact with seven cats at the residence. article.articleHeadline: Diphtheria: Learn about the disease that has reemerged in Brazil and in other countries.
article.articleSummary: Diphtheria reemerges in Brazil and other countries, with PAHO noting that more than half of confirmed cases this year involve individuals who are unvaccinated or have unknown vaccination status. Vaccination coverage against diphtheria remains below ideal levels across the Americas. The disease is caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae and spreads through respiratory droplets. It is characterized by a thick gray pseudomembrane on the throat and tonsils, which can obstruct the airways. If untreated, it can cause severe respiratory distress and damage to the heart and nervous system, with a risk of death. Unvaccinated people or those with incomplete immunization are at greatest risk. The report highlights the ongoing risk and the critical importance of maintaining adequate diphtheria vaccination to curb spread in the region.

article.articleHeadline: Study uses AI to analyze dengue risk by neighborhood in São Paulo.
article.articleSummary: AI-driven project by Instituto Pasteur de São Paulo creates high-resolution dengue transmission risk maps for the city of São Paulo at neighborhood and block scales. It merges climate data (temperature, humidity) with urban socio-environmental indicators—urban heat islands; access to treated water; sewage collection efficiency; and public service coverage—to explain why neighboring areas with similar climates exhibit divergent dengue incidence. The initiative also uses social listening on digital platforms to gauge public and health professionals’ perceptions of dengue vaccine efficacy and safety, aiming to identify collective behavior trends and confidence levels that could affect vaccination uptake, without analyzing individuals. Led by Mauro César Cafundó de Morais, head of the Laboratory of Climate and Health at IPSP (Institute Pasteur of Paris and the University of São Paulo co-founders), with national and international partners. The information originated from Agência de Notícias do Governo do Estado de São Paulo, July 2026; current reference July 11, 2026.

Tests are available without a doctor’s referral at all basic health units Monday–Friday, 8:00–16:00. article.articleHeadline: Anvisa Approves New Pediatric Drug for Chagas Disease.
article.articleSummary: Anvisa approved Lampit (nifurtimox) for treating Chagas disease in children and adolescents up to 17 years, with newborns weighing at least 2.5 kg eligible. This expands treatment options against Trypanosoma cruzi infection in Brazil. In Pará state, a surge of acute Chagas was reported in 2026, notably in Ananindeua; January–March 2026 confirmed 52 cases and five deaths. Transmission is linked to contaminated foods, especially açaí. Lampit is an antiparasitic against T. cruzi, disrupting parasite survival. Transmission routes include the feces of infected triatomine bugs, contaminated foods, blood transfusions, organ transplants, and mother-to-child during pregnancy or birth. Chagas infection has acute and chronic phases; chronic disease can cause severe heart and digestive complications years later. Pediatric approval should broaden early treatment access and reduce progression risk, particularly for infants diagnosed early.

article.articleHeadline: Dengue shifts trend in the Dominican Republic, with cases surpassing 2025 records.
article.articleSummary: Dengue fever in the Dominican Republic reverses a downward trend, with 153 confirmed cases by June 27, 2026—two more than in the same period in 2025. Across the Americas, suspected dengue cases exceed 1.2 million (week 22, 2026), with 337,014 lab-confirmed (about 27%). In DR, 35 cases were confirmed in weeks 22–25, the 10–19 age group most affected and males predominate; DENV-2 is the most frequent serotype. Regional context: 2,294 severe dengue cases and 305 deaths (case fatality 0.025%). Week 22 alone saw 33,405 suspected across 17 countries; 9,249 confirmed, 62 severe, 5 deaths (0.015% fatality). Centroamérica and Mexico reported 1,747 suspected; Costa Rica up 74%. Fifteen countries report circulating dengue serotypes; Brazil, Mexico, and Venezuela report all four serotypes. The Dominican Republic’s shift warrants ongoing epidemiological monitoring, especially among adolescents and young adults.

article.articleHeadline: Acre records more than 500 new tuberculosis cases in 2025.
article.articleSummary: Acre state, Brazil, reported 502 new tuberculosis cases in 2025, with an incidence above the national average of 39.7 per 100,000. Pulmonary TB accounted for 443 cases (88.2%), with 184 women (36.7%) and 318 men (63.3%); 2 cases were recorded post-mortem. Rio Branco logged 285 new TB cases, an incidence of 73.3 per 100,000. In 2024, TB caused 34 deaths in the state: 1 aged 0–14; 22 aged 15–59; and 11 aged 60+. Regional comparison shows Acre’s incidence is lower than Amazonas (93.0) and Pará, Amapá and Roraima (60.0–61.2). TB is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and is primarily pulmonary; transmission is airborne. Diagnostic methods include rapid molecular tests (TRM-TB) or smear, culture, and drug-sensitivity testing, complemented by clinical assessment and chest X-ray. High-risk groups include incarcerated individuals, the elderly, and children/adolescents.

article.articleHeadline: Circulation of DENV-3 Serotype Raises Alarm Over Outbreak Risk
article.articleSummary: Dengue virus serotype 3 (DENV-3) has re-circulated in Acre, Brazil, identified in recent laboratory surveillance, raising public health concern. The Sesacre epidemiological bulletin SE 01–20/2026 reports a substantial reduction in overall dengue incidence in 2026 versus 2025, but simultaneous circulation of dengue serotypes DENV-1, DENV-2 and DENV-3 increases outbreak risk. DENV-2 and DENV-3 circulation remains low, with laboratory-confirmed cases concentrated in Rio Branco through the analyzed period. The bulletin warns that co-circulation heightens the risk of outbreaks and severe dengue in previously infected individuals and calls for intensified epidemiological and laboratory surveillance, vector control, and vaccination. Vaccination coverage is heterogeneous in Acre; the target is to improve complete vaccination (two doses) for children and adolescents aged 10–14 years. article.articleHeadline: Five Dangerous Diseases Caused by Mosquito Bites at Home, Beware
article.articleSummary: Chikungunya, transmitted by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, causes high fever and rash with severe joint pain; no specific vaccine is available currently. Yellow Fever, spread by Aedes and Haemagogus, can cause liver injury with jaundice; vaccination is crucial for people in high-risk areas. Malaria, a Plasmodium infection via female Anopheles mosquitoes, can lead to complications like kidney failure if not treated with artemisinin-based drugs; WHO has approved Mosquirix as an added preventive measure. Filariasis (elephantiasis), caused by filarial worms transmitted by Culex and Mansonia mosquitoes, results in chronic swelling of limbs or genitals if untreated. Zika virus, also spread by Aedes, is typically mild in adults but poses a serious risk for pregnant women due to potential fetal microcephaly. Prevention centers on 3M actions—drain standing water, seal water containers, and recycle waste—plus environmental cleanliness and targeted fogging when mosquito populations rise.

article.articleHeadline: Measures to prevent infection with the Hong Kong influenza virus.
article.articleSummary: Hong Kong influenza virus outbreak in Bali, Indonesia, among expatriates and tourists including Russians, is discussed by Russian virologist Victoria Shirbakova. It is not a new strain but part of the seasonal influenza A cycle, subtype known. High humidity, heat, population density, and ongoing tourism and travel in Asia are cited as factors enabling transmission. Emphasizes adherence to standard preventive measures; incubation can be relatively long; viruses may survive on steel/plastic for days and up to 24 hours on cardboard; aerosols can linger in enclosed spaces for 15–30 minutes. Early treatment is critical because the influenza virus is RNA-based with a replication cycle ~10 hours, and delays permit large viral replication. Antivirals Favipiravir and Molnupiravir inhibit RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, helping curb spread. Supportive care includes antipyretics, decongestants, cough suppressants, fluids, rest, and avoiding exertion.

The policy aims to accelerate case finding and treatment, reducing incidence by targeting transmission sources in the surrounding environment rather than focusing solely on diagnosed patients.

article.articleHeadline: The fight against tuberculosis faces difficulties because many people do not know they are infected.
article.articleSummary: TB remains a major public health challenge as the world aims to end TB by 2030. At APAC-IRIDS 2026 in Thailand, experts warn millions are missed annually; about one-quarter of the population carries latent TB bacteria. In 2024, TB reached 10.7 million cases, with 1.1 million deaths and 2.4 million undiagnosed or unreported; Asia-Pacific region accounted for 6.6 million cases (61%). Late detection and reliance on older tests allow ongoing transmission, including drug-resistant TB. Expanded molecular testing and rapid diagnostics are needed. Preventive strategies must scale up, especially for high-risk groups (household contacts, children under five, people living with HIV, the immunocompromised, diabetics) and latent infection treatment. Many carriers are asymptomatic; chest X-rays can be normal. Integrated screening for TB with HIV, hepatitis C, and diabetes, plus AI-assisted radiology, could shorten diagnosis, but resources, infrastructure, and workforce gaps persist, notably in Pakistan and Indonesia, amid climate-related access challenges.

China and the United States are the leading sources; Soochow University and Capital Medical University are the most active institutions. Publications surged during and after the COVID-19 pandemic, with the top 10 co-cited references including four research articles and six reviews. Current hotspots include epidemiology, diagnostics, macrolide resistance, refractory MPP, and co-infections; COVID-19-related citation bursts are noted. The study highlights the need for stronger global collaboration and more epidemiological studies to address MPP challenges amid evolving infectious threats.

article.articleHeadline: In June, nationwide newly confirmed COVID-19 cases totaled 79,000, of which 130 were severe and 1 person died.
article.articleSummary: China's Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported June COVID-19 activity: 79,000 new infections nationwide across 31 provinces and Xinjiang, with 130 severe cases and 1 death (due to underlying disease). All 3,741 local genome sequences from June 1–30 were Omicron, dominated by NB.1.8.1 and its sublineages; no new variant signaled higher risk. Beijing You An Hospital's Li Tongzeng said cases rose as population immunity wanes; summer indoor cooling and reduced ventilation aid transmission. Symptoms are mostly mild upper-respiratory: fever, sore throat, cough, runny nose; some diarrhea; pneumonia and severe disease remain uncommon. High-risk groups (elderly, chronic disease, immunocompromised) should seek care early and receive antiviral therapy after diagnosis if symptoms occur. From June 29–July 5, ARI surveillance showed activity of influenza, rhinovirus, enterovirus, parainfluenza, and human metapneumovirus; influenza low overall, B-type predominant in the south; rhinovirus down, enterovirus up. Emphasize masking and ventilation.
